title: Foam on the river
hook: form like foam, feeling like bubbles, perception a mirage, formations a hollow stalk, consciousness a magic show (SN 22.95)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the arrow, read whole, and your line, only one arrow. Did you catch the reach for comfort? Today the Buddha sits by the Ganges and points at the water. Day six hundred forty-six.

The Buddha is staying at Ayojjha, on the bank of the Ganges. The river is carrying a big lump of foam downstream. He tells the monks: suppose someone with good eyes looked closely at that foam. Examined it carefully. What would they find? They'd find it empty, hollow, without anything solid inside. Then, one after another, he names four more things a person might see in an ordinary year. Five pictures. Today: foam on the river.
screen: `ON THE BANK OF THE GANGES.` → `A LUMP OF FOAM, FLOATING BY.` → `LOOK CLOSELY: WHAT'S INSIDE?`

segments.voice: SN 22.95 matches each of the five heaps, the parts of a person we met with Vajira's chariot, to something you can see. Form, the body, is like that lump of foam. Feeling is like a bubble. The Buddha sets the scene: in autumn, when it rains in big drops, a bubble rises on the water and bursts. Pleasant, painful, neither: up and gone. Perception, the mind's labeling, is like a mirage in the last month of the hot season, shimmering on the road, convincing, not there. Formations, our habits and intentions, are like a banana tree. A man goes looking for heartwood with a sharp axe. He cuts down a big, straight, young plantain trunk, and peels it, layer after layer, and finds no heartwood at all. Not even softwood. Just layers. And consciousness is like a magic show, a trick put on by a conjurer at a crossroads. Someone with good eyes sees through it. Each picture is chosen carefully. Foam has a shape, but you can't build with it. Bubbles last a moment. A mirage really does look like water. The plantain is layers all the way down. And the magic show doesn't say consciousness isn't happening, it says it isn't what it appears to be. The point isn't gloom. The Buddha says that one who sees this way grows disenchanted, and through dispassion is freed. The verse at the end adds a plain reminder: this body, when life, heat and consciousness leave it, lies cast aside, food for others. Foam, after all, is still beautiful on a river. You just don't try to hold it.
screen: `FORM: A LUMP OF FOAM` · `FEELING: A RAINDROP BUBBLE` · `PERCEPTION: A MIRAGE, FORMATIONS: A PLANTAIN` · `CONSCIOUSNESS: A MAGIC SHOW` · then, large: `FOAM ON THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at foam or bubbles right now: the top of a glass of something fizzy, soap in the sink, a puddle in the rain. If not, picture one clearly. Watch a bubble form, sit, and burst. Then turn to your own feelings as they come, the small pleasant ones, the small unpleasant ones. See each rise and burst, like the raindrops on the river. No need to push any away. Just watch them go. The bell holds the time.
Foam on the river. In SN 22.95, form is foam, feeling a bubble, perception a mirage, formations a plantain trunk, consciousness a magic show. Today's word.
Your line: foam on the river. When a feeling grips you today, picture it as a bubble rising on rainwater, and watch it burst. Day six hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Some Buddhists contemplate the five aggregates through images like these, and teachers in several traditions use the foam, the bubble and the mirage to teach impermanence.

fork.setup: you're looking for heartwood with a sharp axe. you cut down a big plantain trunk and peel it. what do you find?
options: layers, and no heartwood at all.
fork.reveal: just layers, not even softwood: the Buddha's picture of formations, habits and intentions with no solid core.

original.note: Pali phena: foam. SN 22.95 is the Phenapindupama Sutta, the simile of the lump of foam.

trapdoor: what you thought: foam on the river is just a pretty image.
what it means: in SN 22.95, five pictures for the five heaps: foam, bubble, mirage, plantain trunk and magic show, none with a solid core.

what a scholar hears: the foam, bubble and mirage images reappear in later Buddhist literature, including the Dhammapada's verse comparing the world to a bubble and a mirage, and the Mahayana's Diamond Sutra.

notes: SN 22.95 paraphrased. Confirm the setting (Ayojjha on the bank of the Ganges), the five similes in order and their details (bubble in autumn when it rains in big drops; mirage in the last month of the hot season; a young plantain trunk cut down by a man seeking heartwood; a magic illusion displayed by a magician or his apprentice at a crossroads), and the closing verse about the body cast aside when life, heat and consciousness depart.
